    • FX MORNING NOTES

    GS FX Research Notes: Japanese Portfolio Flows: Still No Signs of Rotation Among Unhedged Investors—But Hedged Investors Have Been Selling Foreign Bonds

    Research | Economics | 8 October 2026 | 8:53AM UTC

    We recently turned structurally bullish Yen as the domestic policies that have weighed on the currency for much of the past 10-15 years appear to be shifting in a more supportive direction. The BoJ has seemingly shifted to a faster pace of hikes and, most importantly, there appears to be a focus within the government on encouraging some reallocation by domestic investors back towards domestic assets.

    As a result, investor attention has turned to the monthly International Transactions in Securities (ITS) data to watch for any signs of reduced demand for foreign assets by key investors. We have been of the view that any shift in flows would likely be a slower-moving process, and so far that looks true among mostly unhedged investors.

    The trust accounts category, which includes the public pension fund, suggests that net purchases of foreign bonds continued in September, but at a slower pace than in August ($7.6bn vs $14.7bn in August) and below the average pace of the prior six months ($8.6bn).

    In contrast, the investment trusts category, which includes retail investors and NISA account flows, suggests that net purchases of foreign equities accelerated slightly in September to $8.7bn (vs. $8.5bn in August)—reflecting continued strong demand for other markets.

    More broadly, our preferred estimate of key unhedged investor flows suggests that demand for foreign assets has generally persisted at a similar pace over the past year and shows no obvious signs of rotation. If that were to change, however, these data would be the first place to see it.

    While less relevant for the Yen, repatriation flows have been evident in the data for typically hedged investors (mainly banks and roughly 40% of flows by Lifers). Net sales of foreign bonds by banks accelerated from $8.3bn in August in September to $15.9bn. Lifers also net sold slightly more foreign bonds in September than in August ($1.9bn vs $0.9bn). While monthly flows can be somewhat volatile, the trend in total 12-month flows looks increasingly negative—similar to the period of rising global yields in 2022. These data also predate the sudden volatility in the European bond market over the past week, and France represents the biggest share of Japan’s foreign debt holdings after the US (see Exhibit 2 here).
